entry: Compact assembly of electronic circuits, also called a microchip or chip, fabricated on a thin, flat piece of [[Semiconductor|semiconductor]] material, usually [[Silicon|silicon]]. Integrated circuits perform functions such as data processing, control, memory and power management in [[Computer|computers]], [[Smartphone|smartphones]] and televisions. Compared with circuits built from discrete components, they are smaller, faster, cheaper and more energy-efficient, because whole circuits are printed as a unit by photolithography. Their main disadvantage is the high initial cost of design and factory construction, so they are commercially viable only when high production volumes are anticipated. Progress has roughly followed [[Moore's law]]: a modern chip may hold many billions of [[Transistor|transistors]] in an area the size of a human fingernail. [[Jack Kilby]] conceived the idea in 1958, and Robert Noyce developed a silicon-based version in 1959.

Technique of [[Calculus|calculus]] for integrating a product of two functions. It is derived from the product rule of differentiation and states that the integral of u dv equals uv minus the integral of v du. It is frequently used to transform an integral that is hard to evaluate into one that is easier to solve. Brook Taylor published the idea in 1715. The discrete analogue for [[Sequence|sequences]] is called summation by parts.

Set of organs forming the outermost layer of an animal's body, including the [[Skin|skin]], [[Hair|hair]], scales, [[Feather|feathers]], hooves, claws and [[Nail (anatomy)|nails]]. It acts as a protective barrier between the external and internal environment, maintains water balance, excretes waste and regulates [[Temperature|body temperature]]. Its sensory receptors detect pain, sensation, pressure and temperature. The skin has two major layers, the outermost epidermis and the inner dermis, separated by a basement membrane. The epidermis has four to five layers, and the dermis contains connective tissues, blood vessels, glands, hair roots and nerve endings. In humans the skin accounts for about 12 to 15 percent of total body weight and covers 1.5 to 2 m² of surface area. The skin also synthesizes [[Vitamin D|vitamin D]] in the epidermis upon exposure to UVB radiation.

American multinational technology company headquartered in Santa Clara, California. It designs and sells [[Central processing unit|central processing units]] and related products, and it is one of the developers of the [[X86|x86]] instruction set found in most [[Personal computer|personal computers]]. Founded in 1968 by Gordon Moore, Robert Noyce and Arthur Rock, it released the Intel 4004 in 1971, the world's first commercial microprocessor chip. During the 1990s its partnership with [[Microsoft Windows|Microsoft Windows]] shaped the PC market, and competition from [[AMD|AMD]] has since reduced its dominance.

Category of property that includes intangible creations of the human intellect. Intellectual property rights give creators or owners the right to use an asset and to prevent others from doing so. The best-known types are [[Patent|patents]], [[Copyright|copyrights]], trademarks and trade secrets. Supporters argue that these protections give creators economic incentives to produce and innovate. Because intellectual goods can be consumed by an unlimited number of people without being depleted, balancing rights strong enough to encourage creation against rights that limit wide use is the primary focus of modern law. The Venetian Patent Statute of March 19, 1474, established by the [[Republic of Venice|Republic of Venice]], is usually considered the earliest codified patent system. Britain's Statute of Anne (1710) is seen as the origin of copyright.

Total score from standardized tests designed to assess human intelligence. Modern IQ tests transform raw scores to a [[Normal distribution|normal distribution]] with a mean of 100 and a [[Standard deviation|standard deviation]] of 15, so about two-thirds of people score between 85 and 115. IQ scores are estimates of intelligence, which, unlike distance or mass, cannot be measured directly. They have been associated with factors such as nutrition and parental socioeconomic status, and they are used for educational placement and for evaluating job applicants. Raw scores have risen by an average of three points per decade since the early 20th century, a phenomenon called the Flynn effect.

Form of [[Agriculture|agriculture]], of crops and animals, with high levels of input and output per unit of land area. It is characterized by a low fallow ratio, heavy use of capital, labor, [[Fertilizer|fertilizers]], [[Pesticide|pesticides]] and water, and higher crop yields. Modern methods often use antibiotics for livestock, and intensive farms are widespread in developed nations. Intensive animal farming raises large numbers of animals on a relatively small area, either through rotational grazing or in concentrated animal feeding operations. The [[Green Revolution|Green Revolution]] of the 1960s expanded yields through high-yielding crop varieties, irrigation and chemical inputs. Critics cite water and soil contamination, [[Greenhouse gas|greenhouse gas]] emissions, reduced [[Biodiversity|biodiversity]] and antimicrobial resistance. Some intensive farms use sustainable methods, although these typically require more labor or lower yields.

Football club, formally Football Club Internazionale Milano, based in [[Milan|Milan]], Lombardy. Founded on March 9, 1908, after a split within the Milan Foot-Ball and Cricket Club (now [[AC Milan|AC Milan]]), it is the only team to have an unbroken presence in [[Serie A|Serie A]] since its 1909 debut. It has won 21 league titles and three [[UEFA Champions League|Champions League]] titles, and it shared the San Siro stadium with AC Milan from 1947. In 2010 it completed an unprecedented Italian treble. Oaktree Capital Management has owned the club since May 2024.

Components made to specifications so nearly identical that any one can replace another without custom fitting. This interchangeability allows easy assembly of new devices and repair of existing ones, minimizing the time and skill required. It made the [[Assembly line|assembly line]] possible at the beginning of the 20th century. Evidence of the practice dates back over two thousand years to [[Carthage|Carthage]] in the First Punic War, when ships had standardized parts marked for assembly. In the late 18th century, French General Jean-Baptiste Vaquette de Gribeauval promoted standardized weapons, and by around 1778 Honoré Blanc was producing firearms with interchangeable flintlock mechanisms. Industrial production developed in the United States in the 19th century, where it was called the American system of manufacturing. Advances in machine tools, jigs, fixtures and gauges made it practical.

Ballistic missile with a range greater than 5,500 km (3,400 mi), primarily designed to deliver [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]]. Many carry multiple independently targetable reentry vehicles (MIRVs), allowing one missile to strike several targets. The [[United States|United States]], [[Russia|Russia]], [[China|China]], France, India, the [[United Kingdom|United Kingdom]], Israel and [[North Korea|North Korea]] are the only countries known to have operational ICBMs. The first, the R-7 Semyorka, was tested in 1957. Early designs used liquid propellants that required fueling before launch, while solid-propellant designs need no fueling and respond far faster.

Payment above the principal sum of a loan or deposit, made at a particular rate. A borrower pays interest to a lender, and a saver may earn it from a bank. Interest differs from [[Profit (economics)|profit]], which goes to the owner of an asset or enterprise, and from a dividend, which a company pays from profit without a fixed rate. The rate of interest is the amount paid or received over a period divided by the principal, usually expressed as a percentage. Compound interest is earned on prior interest as well as principal, so debt grows exponentially, and its mathematical study led to the discovery of the number [[E (mathematical constant)|e]]. The [[First Council of Nicaea|First Council of Nicaea]] in 325 forbade clergy from usury, defined as lending on interest above 1 percent per month. [[Thomas Aquinas|St. Thomas Aquinas]] argued that charging interest was "double charging", charging for both the thing and its use.

Technique that uses the interference of superimposed waves to extract information. Interferometers usually split light from a single source into two beams that travel different optical paths and then recombine them, so the resulting fringes reveal the difference in path lengths. They are widely used to measure microscopic displacements, refractive index changes and surface irregularities. In analytical science they measure lengths and the shape of optical components with nanometer precision, making them the highest-precision length measuring instruments in existence. Interferometry is important in [[Astronomy|astronomy]], [[Seismology|seismology]], [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopy]], [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]] and [[Radiology|radiology]]. An astronomical interferometer combines two or more separate dishes, offering a resolution equal to that of a single telescope whose diameter equals the largest separation between them. [[Albert A. Michelson|Albert A. Michelson]] developed the Michelson interferometer for precise length measurements in the late 1800s.

Art and science of enhancing the interior of a building to create a healthier and more aesthetically pleasing environment. An interior designer plans, researches, coordinates and manages such projects, which may include space planning, site inspections, programming, construction management and execution of the design. The profession draws on fundamental principles from the [[Visual arts|visual arts]]. It is separate from interior decoration, a term more common in the U.S.; in the U.K., interior design is still unregulated. Painting interior walls has existed for at least 5,000 years, and the Greeks and later Romans added decorative [[Mosaic|mosaic]] floors. In the mid-to-late 19th century, a growing [[Middle class|middle class]] created demand for furnished interiors, and the modern profession emerged in the mid-20th century.

Word or expression that occurs on its own and expresses a spontaneous feeling, situation or reaction. Interjections include exclamations such as ouch and wow, curses, [[Greeting|greetings]], response particles such as okay, and hesitation markers such as uh and um. Most express feeling rather than representing an idea. Volitive interjections make requests, as in shh, emotive ones express emotions such as disgust, and cognitive ones express thought or confusion. Greek grammarians classed interjections as [[Adverb|adverbs]] that modified verbs, but many Latin scholars treated them as an independent part of speech. Primary interjections, such as oops and ouch, are interjections first; secondary ones, such as damn, come from other word classes.

Force of attraction or repulsion between molecules and neighboring particles such as atoms or ions. Intermolecular forces are weak relative to the intramolecular forces, such as [[Covalent bond|covalent bonds]], that hold a molecule together. They hold particles together in liquids and solids and determine properties such as melting and boiling points, [[Viscosity|viscosity]] and solubility. Attractive types include [[Hydrogen bond|hydrogen bonding]], ion–dipole forces, cation–π bonding and [[Van der Waals force|van der Waals forces]], which include the London dispersion force. A hydrogen bond links a hydrogen atom, bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine, to another such atom. It is directional and stronger than a van der Waals interaction. Information on these forces comes from macroscopic measurements of properties such as pressure, volume and temperature.

Energy that defines the state of a thermodynamic system, excluding the kinetic energy of its overall motion and the effects of external fields. It is a state variable: it depends only on the internal state of the system, not on the process by which energy enters or leaves. The total internal energy cannot practically be measured, so thermodynamics concerns changes in it. These changes arise from energy transferred as [[Heat|heat]] or thermodynamic work, or from transfers of matter. Without a process, the internal energy of an isolated system does not change, a principle that underlies the [[First law of thermodynamics|first law of thermodynamics]], as formulated by Rudolf Clausius. In statistical mechanics it is analyzed through the kinetic energies of microscopic motion and the potential energies of microscopic forces, including [[Chemical bond|chemical bonds]]. The [[Joule|joule]] is the SI unit of energy.

Intergovernmental organization that promotes the peaceful use of nuclear energy and inhibits its use for military purposes, including [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]]. It was established in 1957 as an autonomous organization within the [[United Nations|United Nations]] system and is headquartered at the UN Office at [[Vienna|Vienna]], Austria. It was created amid rising tensions between the United States and the [[Soviet Union|Soviet Union]], and U.S. president [[Dwight D. Eisenhower|Dwight D. Eisenhower]]'s "Atoms for Peace" speech is credited with catalyzing its formation. The agency verifies through safeguards that nuclear energy is not used for military purposes, promotes nuclear safety and security standards, and provides technical training, particularly in the developing world. Following ratification of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons in 1968, non-nuclear powers were required to negotiate safeguards agreements with it. In 2005, the agency and its director general, Mohamed ElBaradei, were awarded the Nobel Peace Prize.

Principal judicial organ of the [[United Nations|United Nations]], seated at the Peace Palace in [[The Hague|The Hague]], Netherlands. Established in June 1945 by the UN Charter, it began work in April 1946 as the successor to the Permanent Court of International Justice, which the [[League of Nations|League of Nations]] had set up in 1920. It settles legal disputes submitted by states and gives advisory opinions on legal questions, and its rulings serve as primary sources of [[International law|international law]]. Its 15 judges are elected for nine-year terms, and no two may be nationals of the same country. Its judgments are binding and final, but the court has no formal enforcement mechanism, so enforcement is a political matter for the UN Security Council, where the five permanent members hold veto power.

headword: International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights
sort_key: international covenant on civil and political rights
entry: Multilateral treaty that commits nations to respect individuals' civil and political rights, including the right to life, [[Freedom of religion|freedom of religion]], [[Freedom of speech|freedom of speech]], freedom of assembly, electoral rights and the right to due process and a fair trial. The United Nations General Assembly adopted it on December 16, 1966, and it entered into force on March 23, 1976. It forms part of the International Bill of Human Rights, along with the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights|Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] and the [[International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights|International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights]]. As of December 2025 the treaty had 175 parties, and six more signatories had not ratified it, including [[China|China]] and [[Cuba|Cuba]]. The Human Rights Committee reviews reports from states parties, which usually report every four years when the committee requests them.

headword: International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights
sort_key: international covenant on economic social and cultural rights
entry: Multilateral treaty adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on December 16, 1966, committing its parties to work toward economic, social and cultural rights for all individuals. The rights include labor rights, the right to form and join [[Trade union|trade unions]], the right to health, the right to education and the right to an adequate standard of living. Its first article recognizes the right of all peoples to [[Self-determination|self-determination]]. Parties implement the rights progressively, and the rights may be limited only by law for the purpose of promoting the general welfare in a democratic society. The covenant entered into force on January 3, 1976. Four more signatories, including the United States, have not ratified it. It is part of the International Bill of Human Rights, together with the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights|Universal Declaration of Human Rights]] and the [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights|International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]].

Intergovernmental organization and international tribunal seated in [[The Hague|The Hague]], Netherlands. Established in 2002 under the Rome Statute, it is the first and only permanent international court with jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and aggression. It acts only when national courts are unwilling or unable to prosecute. As of October 2024, 125 states were parties to the Rome Statute, while [[China|China]], [[India|India]], [[Russia|Russia]] and the [[United States|United States]] do not recognize its jurisdiction. Critics question its legitimacy, its reliance on state cooperation for arrests and the high cost of its proceedings.

Line that marks the boundary between one calendar day and the next, extending between the North and South Poles. It roughly follows the 180° meridian through the [[Pacific Ocean|Pacific Ocean]], deviating to pass around some territories and island groups. Crossing it eastbound decreases the date by one day, and crossing it westbound increases the date. The line is a cartographic convention that international law does not define, so countries through whose waters it passes have at times moved it for convenience. The line swings far east around [[Kiribati|Kiribati]], whose easternmost islands have the latest time on Earth, UTC+14:00. [[Howland Island|Howland Island]] and Baker Island, just north of the equator, have the earliest time, UTC−12:00.

International financial institution and specialized agency of the United Nations, headquartered in [[Washington, D.C.|Washington, D.C.]] It has 191 member countries and aims to foster global monetary cooperation, secure financial stability, facilitate international trade, promote high employment and reduce poverty. Established at the Bretton Woods Conference in July 1944, on ideas from Harry Dexter White and [[John Maynard Keynes|John Maynard Keynes]], it came into formal existence in 1945 with 29 member countries. The IMF acts as a lender of last resort to members experiencing balance-of-payments crises. A quota system determines both each member's contribution and its voting power. Loans often require borrowing countries to adopt policy reforms, known as structural adjustment. Critics argue that these conditions impose austerity that can harm the most vulnerable and limit economic sovereignty, and that Western countries dominate its governance.

Alphabetic system of phonetic notation, based primarily on the [[Latin script|Latin script]]. It was devised by the International Phonetic Association, which a group of French and English language teachers led by the French linguist Paul Passy formed in 1886 and which was known by that name from 1897. The alphabet is a standard written representation of [[Speech|speech]] sounds used by [[Linguistics|linguists]], lexicographers, language teachers, speech–language pathologists, singers and translators. It represents qualities of speech such as phones, intonation and the separation of [[Syllable|syllables]]. Segments are transcribed with letters and diacritics, and slashes signal phonemic transcription. Since its most recent addition in 2005, the alphabet has 107 segmental letters, augmented by tone letters and diacritics.

Modular space station in [[Low Earth orbit|low Earth orbit]], operated by five partner agencies: [[NASA|NASA]] of the United States, [[Roscosmos|Roscosmos]] of Russia, ESA, JAXA and CSA. It is the first space station built, maintained and crewed through international cooperation, and the largest human spacecraft ever constructed. It orbits between 51.64° north and south at about 400 km (250 miles) above Earth, circling roughly every 93 minutes. Its modules support scientific research in microgravity, crew habitation, storage and spacecraft control, and its eight docking ports serve visiting spacecraft. Continuous human occupancy began on November 2, 2000, the longest continuous human presence in space. As of August 2025, 290 individuals from 26 countries had visited it. Alongside China's Tiangong, it is one of two operational space stations.
